## Introduction

Glaucoma is a degenerative optic neuropathy characterized by the loss of retinal ganglion cells and vision loss. It affects >50 million people and is considered the second-leading cause of blindness worldwide.1,2 The pathophysiology underlying primary open-angle glaucoma (OAG), the most common form of glaucoma, is incompletely understood, but is associated with an increase in intraocular pressure (IOP). An increase in IOP is thought to damage the retinal ganglion cell layer and cause vision loss that can be irreversible.3 Although several new alternative glaucoma treatment modalities centering on neuroprotection and axonal regeneration have been discussed in recent years as a complement to IOP-lowering therapy,4 there remain three primary treatment modalities targeting IOP reduction in patients with OAG: topical drops, laser procedures, and incisional surgery. Topical drops modulate the production and drainage of aqueous humor, the primary fluid constituent that contributes to IOP. In contrast, laser procedures and incisional procedures ablate or reform the tissues comprising the aqueous drainage pathway to improve outflow facility and fluid egress.

The corneal endothelium comprises the most posterior tissue layer of the cornea and consists of a single sheet of cells that acts to maintain corneal transparency through modulation of corneal hydration. In the human cornea, endothelial cells are postmitotic and therefore are especially susceptible to injury or insult. Given the proximity between angle structures and the cornea,

# Decoding Corneal Endothelial Loss from Glaucoma Treatment: A Case-Control Stratification Analysis

Christopher D Yang1 , Blaze Ann C Carbonell2, Vincent Hussey3, Anjali A Herekar4, Christine K Kim5, David M Morcos6, Andrew K Smith7, Austin R Fox8, Sameh Mosaed9, Ken Y Lin10, Olivia L Lee11

Received on: 04 December 2024; Accepted on: 28 December 2024; Published on: 31 July 2025

## Abstract

Aim and background: To characterize the effects of glaucoma treatment on the corneal endothelium by quantifying corneal endothelial morphology in eyes with and without glaucoma using in vivo specular microscopy. Materials and methods: This is a case-control study of 304 eyes conducted at an ambulatory glaucoma clinic at a tertiary academic institution from August 2021 through July 2023. Primary outcomes include endothelial cell density (ECD), coefficient of variation (CV), and hexagonality (Hex). Images of the central corneal endothelium were obtained using a non-contact Konan NSP-9000 specular microscope (Konan Medical, Irvine, CA, United States). The highest quality image of each cornea was selected for analysis. Each corneal endothelial image was manually graded using the Center Method and analyzed using CellChek (Konan Medical, Irvine, CA, United States) software. Results: Glaucomatous eyes demonstrate significantly lower corneal ECD compared to control eyes and glaucoma suspect eyes. Topical glaucoma drop use, trabeculectomy, and glaucoma tube shunt surgery independently predict a significant reduction in corneal ECD. Alpha agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (CAI), and Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor drops independently predict a significant reduction in corneal ECD, with ROCK inhibitors predicting the greatest absolute decrease. Conclusion: Eyes treated with topical drops, trabeculectomy, or glaucoma tube shunt implantation demonstrate lower corneal ECD compared to control eyes. Use of topical drops from the alpha agonist, CAI, and ROCK inhibitor classes predicts significant corneal endothelial cell loss. Clinical significance: These findings provide valuable clinical context for the medical management of glaucoma that may reduce adverse outcomes and preserve corneal function in patients receiving ocular hypotensive therapy. Keywords: Corneal endothelium, Endothelial cell density, Glaucoma, Glaucoma medication, Glaucoma surgery. Journal of Current Glaucoma Practice (2025): 10.5005/jp-journals-10078-1463

Images were independently analyzed by two masked graders who underwent the same image analysis training protocol. Manually labeled images were then processed using CellChek (Konan Medical, Irvine, CA, United States), yielding ECD, CV, and Hex values.

Chart Review Participant demographic variables and ophthalmic history were collected via filtered search of the UC Irvine Health electronic medical record (EMR). Glaucoma staging and severity were defined using International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes. Chart reviewers were trained to collect necessary data points from the EMR and utilized a standardized data acquisition template, including age, sex, phakic status, glaucoma severity, glaucoma treatment history, and ophthalmologic comorbidities that was developed a priori. After preliminary data collection, chart reviewers removed erroneous data or missing data points.

Statistical Analysis Data were analyzed using SPSS 28.0 (IBM Corp; Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics were run to evaluate the baseline characteristics of study participants. One-way ANOVA was used to assess differences in corneal ECD, CV, and Hex between control eyes, glaucoma suspect eyes, and glaucomatous eyes. Glaucoma suspect and glaucomatous eyes were then categorized by treatment modality, which included topical drops, laser procedures, microinvasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS), trabeculectomy, and glaucoma tube shunt surgery. Multivariate logistic regression was used to evaluate differences in corneal ECD between glaucoma treatment groups and between benzalkonium chloride (BAK)- containing and non-BAK-containing glaucoma medications. Multivariate linear regression was used to interrogate the effect of different glaucoma medication classes on corneal ECD. Associations are reported as effect sizes.

## Results

The baseline characteristics of the eyes included in this study are presented in Table 1. A total of 84 control eyes (29.47%), 24 glaucoma suspect eyes (8.42%), and 177 glaucomatous eyes (62.11%) were enrolled. The average age of study participants was 67.32 years. Most study participants were male (52.98%). Chi-squared analysis revealed no differences in sex (p = 0.210) or phakic status (p = 0.068) between these same groups. Therefore, specular microscopy is a powerful tool capable of empirically assessing the effects of medical and surgical glaucoma treatment on the corneal endothelium.

While glaucoma therapies are critical for preventing glaucomatous vision loss, their effects on the corneal endothelium remain poorly understood. The present study aims to characterize the effects of glaucoma treatment, especially topical glaucoma drops, on the corneal endothelium by characterizing corneal endothelial morphology in eyes with and without glaucoma using in vivo specular microscopy. Understanding the side effects of commonly used glaucoma therapies will provide useful clinical evidence that may inform treatment recommendations for patients with glaucomatous vision loss.

Materials and Methods Patient Enrollment All patients in this case-control study were recruited from the ambulatory glaucoma clinic at the Gavin Herbert Eye Institute between August 2021 and July 2023. Patients with diagnosed glaucoma, glaucoma suspect, and control patients without a glaucoma-related diagnosis were considered eligible for inclusion. Exclusion criteria included corneal or intraocular surgery within the last 6 months or a prior history of corneal disease or penetrating keratoplasty. Patients who had changes to their glaucoma medication regimen or received laser treatment or incisional surgery for glaucoma within the last 6 months were also excluded. Patients who consented to study enrollment were eligible for inclusion, regardless of visual acuity or glaucoma stage. 285 eyes met criteria for inclusion during this study, of which 84 were controls. Informed consent was obtained from all study participants in accordance with the UC Irvine Office of Research under IRB#20195254. All human subjects research adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Image Acquisition Images of the central corneal endothelium were obtained using a non-contact NSP-9000 specular microscope (Konan Medical, Irvine, CA, United States). At least two images per eye were collected. Image quality was screened by two masked graders with reference to Image Quality Rating (IQR), an index of specular microscopy image gradability.6 The highest quality images were selected for downstream processing and quantitative analysis.

Image Analysis Each corneal endothelial image was manually labeled using the Center Method,7 an image approximation method that labels the center of corneal endothelial cells in a concentric fashion.

The effects of different classes of topical glaucoma drops on corneal ECD were then interrogated via linear regression analysis of corneal ECD using different topical glaucoma drop classes as independent covariates (Table 4). Glaucoma drops were subcategorized into the following classes: beta-blockers, prostaglandin analogs, alpha agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAI), and Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitors. The regression model was significant overall (p < 0.001) and revealed that alpha agonist (β = –251.103, p = 0.002), CAI (β = –188.689, p = 0.032), and ROCK inhibitor (β = –319.399, p = 0.025) medications all independently predict a significant reduction in corneal ECD, with ROCK inhibitors predicting the greatest absolute decrease in corneal ECD. Notably, beta blockers (β = 76.755, p = 0.403) and prostaglandin analogs (β = 20.682, p = 0.831) were both associated with an absolute increase in ECD, but these associations were not statistically significant.

To evaluate the relationship between baseline glaucoma severity and corneal ECD, we performed a linear regression analysis incorporating the different glaucoma treatment modalities as independent covariates. This analysis revealed no significant association between glaucoma severity and ECD (Table 5). We then conducted a separate linear regression analysis of BAK-containing drops and non-BAK-containing drops. The regression model was significant overall (p < 0.001; Table 6) and revealed a more pronounced but statistically insignificant decrease in corneal ECD with BAK-containing drops (β = –227.794, p = 0.103) compared to non-BAK-containing drops (β = –176.198, p = 0.169).

Our observation that prior trabeculectomy13,16 and prior glaucoma tube shunt surgery17,18 independently predict a significant reduction in corneal ECD is consistent with previously published reports in the literature.

Prior studies have reported transient increases in central corneal thickness with alpha agonist use in vivo,19 but the effects of this medication class on corneal ECD are not fully understood. We find that chronic alpha agonist use predicts a significant reduction in corneal ECD. This observation suggests this medication class is cytotoxic to the corneal endothelium over a chronic time scale. As alpha agonists are either used independently in cases where stabilization of IOP is desired or in combined drop formulations that combine multiple pharmacologic classes,20 the fact that their use predicts corneal endothelial loss should be considered when prescribing medications in the context of individualized ophthalmologic comorbidities and risk factors.

On the contrary, CAIs are thought to exert their ocular hypotensive effect by suppressing aqueous humor production at the level of the ciliary process.21 The corneal endothelium expresses the carbonic anhydrase I and II isoenzymes, both of which regulate fluid transport in the anterior chamber to maintain corneal hydration.22 Previously published randomized-controlled trials23 and prospective studies24 identify a positive association between CAIs and corneal thickness but no significant association with corneal ECD; this finding has largely been attributed to a reduction in endothelial pump function with CAI use. In the present study, we find that CAI use predicts a significant reduction in corneal ECD. This observation is consistent with the previously established association between this medication class and corneal edema.22,25 Prior studies in the cornea literature have identified a temporal relationship between endothelial cell loss and increased corneal thickness after cataract surgery.26,27 It is reasonable that decreased

## Discussion

Treatment of glaucoma with topical drops is considered the most practical first-line therapy due to ease of access, safety, and efficacy. Clinicians typically prescribe topical glaucoma medications from one of five drug classes: prostaglandin analogs, beta-blockers, CAIs, alpha adrenergic agonists, and ROCK inhibitors.8 The detrimental effects of laser procedures and incisional glaucoma on corneal endothelial health are well understood.9–12 In contrast, despite their prevalence, the effects of topical glaucoma drops on the corneal endothelium remain understudied. Currently published data are equivocal, with several studies reporting no significant change in corneal ECD after years of chronic glaucoma drop administration13,14 and others reporting significant but often conflicting changes in corneal ECD with chronic glaucoma drop use.15,13 One review paper synthesizing the current body of evidence on glaucoma drops and their effects on corneal ECD exemplifies this discrepancy, reporting that drops from the beta-blocker and carbonic anhydrase classes appear to marginally reduce corneal ECD, but that these effects still remain unclear.15

The present study evaluates the effects of different glaucoma treatments on corneal ECD in eyes controlled for age, sex, and phakic status. We find that prior topical glaucoma drop use, prior trabeculectomy, and prior glaucoma tube shunt surgery independently predict a significant reduction in corneal ECD. Subgroup analysis of topical glaucoma drop classes reveals that alpha agonist, CAI, and ROCK inhibitor medications are all independent predictors of significant endothelial cell loss, with ROCK inhibitors displaying the most significant reduction. about the safety of BAK-containing drops due to their association with ocular surface disease.40 Prior in vitro studies of BAK-containing drops demonstrate a dose-dependent toxicity in cultured corneal endothelial cells.41 In the present study, we discovered that BAKcontaining drops predict a nonsignificant reduction in corneal ECD compared to drops without BAK. In summary, it appears that ocular hypotensive drugs that contain BAK or are from the beta-blocker or prostaglandin analog classes are not associated with corneal endothelial changes.

There are several limitations to our study. First, we did not incorporate duration of medical treatment into our regression model. Withholding this information from our analysis precludes a deeper understanding of a potential temporal association between topical glaucoma drop use and corneal endothelial loss. Likewise, we did not quantify the relationship between length of postprocedure follow-up and corneal ECD for patients who received laser or surgical procedures for glaucoma. Second, there is an established association between glaucoma itself and corneal endothelial cell loss.42 We did not derive any conclusive evidence supporting or refuting this association, as our institution is a tertiary care center and does not include a sizable population of treatmentnaive patients. Therefore, we did not include such a control group in our study. Subgroup analysis of glaucoma suspect eyes based on the presence or absence of prior medical therapy could clarify this association and is a worthy area of future investigation. Third, we did not incorporate IOP maximums and minimums in our analysis, barring a deeper understanding of how glaucoma itself affects corneal ECD. There is also a known age-related decline in corneal ECD that may confound the findings observed in our study. Our control and case groups exhibited a borderline significant difference in average age despite having numerically similar ages (Table 1). Although we made efforts to minimize these age-related differences, they were not systematic. Future studies incorporating these points would add value to our findings and provide needed clarity to best practices surrounding glaucoma management.

The increasingly versatile armamentarium of glaucoma treatment modalities, both medical and surgical, allows modern ophthalmologists to provide more personalized glaucoma care based on IOP reduction goals and the unique anatomic and glaucomatous characteristics of each eye. Common first- and second-line glaucoma treatments, including topical drops, in-office laser procedures, and MIGS, are associated with mild or no reduction in ECD. While our data herein show that some topical drop classes—namely, alpha agonists, CAIs, and ROCK inhibitors— are associated with lower ECD, the largest reduction in ECD is associated with third- and fourth-line glaucoma treatments such as topical netarsudil, trabeculectomy, and glaucoma tube shunt surgery. Our interpretation of these findings is not that topical drops, trabeculectomies, or glaucoma tube shunt surgery should be avoided entirely; nor do we endorse electing for immediate laser procedures or MIGS instead of titrating medical therapy in patients with mild-to-moderate glaucoma. Rather, we believe that careful assessment of the risks and benefits of each glaucoma treatment modality should be incorporated in every patient’s management. We encourage the use of specular microscopy at the point of care to understand the status of the corneal endothelium and encourage personalized and patient-centered treatment. IOP control remains a top priority; nevertheless, an understanding of the risks of each treatment, including, but not limited to, the effects on the corneal endothelium, should be considered.

ECD observed in eyes treated with CAIs in the present study occurs through a similar downstream pathophysiologic mechanism. Regardless, our observation that chronic CAI drop use predicts corneal endothelial loss is clinically relevant and should guide future medication decision-making for patients with glaucomatous vision changes.

Chronic use of drops from the beta-blocker or prostaglandin analog classes for ocular hypotensive therapy was not found to predict corneal endothelial cell loss in our study. Prior studies investigating the effects of chronic topical beta-blocker drops on the corneal endothelium are equivocal.28,29 To date, there is no established clinical evidence of corneal endothelial cell loss in eyes treated with beta-blocker drops. Similarly, there are few studies examining the effects of prostaglandin analogs on the corneal endothelium, though the current evidence suggests chronic topical prostaglandin analog use does not affect corneal ECD.30 Published data characterize a relationship between topical beta-blocker use and corneal thickness.31,32 Notably, beta-blocker and prostaglandin analog drops are universally considered first- or second-line medical therapy for the treatment of glaucoma, and therefore, patients on these drops likely have fewer baseline corneal endothelial derangements compared to those on alpha agonists or ROCK inhibitors.

Rho-associated protein kinase inhibitors represent a newer class of ocular hypotensive medications that are usually employed as third- or fourth-line medical treatment in cases of intractable ocular hypertension. They reduce IOP by inhibiting the contractile tissues of the trabecular meshwork and thereby increasing aqueous outflow.33 In the present study, we find that ROCK inhibitors are associated with the most significant corneal endothelial cell loss of any glaucoma medication class. This finding contradicts previously published work demonstrating an association between ROCK inhibitors and enhanced corneal endothelial proliferation in vitro,34 in animals,35 and in humans.36 There is accumulating evidence that ROCK inhibitors can be used therapeutically to regenerate the corneal endothelium in patients with Fuchs’ dystrophy, an inherited keratopathy characterized by progressive corneal endothelial loss and edema.37,38 Our finding that ROCK inhibitors predict corneal endothelial loss is surprising in this context. However, it is important to note that given their status as a lastresort medication, ROCK inhibitors are used more often in patients who are more likely to have baseline corneal endothelial loss due to intractable ocular hypertension or spikes in IOP. Nevertheless, our multivariate analysis shows no significant relationship between glaucoma severity and endothelial cell. Despite this, our observed association between ROCK inhibitors and corneal endothelial loss does not prove causality. Moreover, studies reporting promotion of corneal regeneration with ROCK inhibitor treatment primarily evaluate ripasudil, fasudil, and other investigational ROCK inhibitor medications not approved in the United States. Notably, our study included only one ROCK inhibitor, netarsudil, which has known secondary activity as a norepinephrine transporter inhibitor.39 This off-target activity may contribute to our seemingly contradictory finding that netarsudil use is associated with corneal endothelial cell loss. Regardless, that netarsudil is associated with a decrease in ECD over time warrants further investigation.

## Conclusion

Glaucomatous eyes, particularly those treated with topical drops, trabeculectomy, or tube shunt, exhibit lower corneal ECD compared to normal controls. Chronic use of topical drops from the alpha agonist, CAI, and ROCK inhibitor classes predicts significant corneal endothelial loss. This loss in the absence of change in CV or Hex may be caused by glaucoma treatment, glaucoma itself, or a combination of both. Although we found no significant association between glaucoma severity and ECD, the medication classes found to be associated with reduced ECD in our study are typically employed in eyes with advanced glaucoma severity. These findings should inform clinical decision-making regarding glaucoma management, particularly in eyes at risk for corneal decompensation.
